appendix_digests.title: A Checklist for the Four Stages of Writing

claims.claim: Before organizing, clarify purpose and readers, allocate time across the process, research broadly, take source-aware notes, and push beyond the first obvious ideas.
Write specific main propositions, order them deliberately, plan the opening and conclusion, and decide whether any visual aid would clarify the case.
Reduce distractions, draft from the outline, begin with a tractable point, complete substantial units in one sitting where possible, and postpone polishing.

After a complete draft, first identify missing development, allow distance if time permits, reread as the audience, fix the two largest weaknesses, and then test completeness, emphasis, clarity, transitions, concision, specificity, interest, phrasing, punctuation, and typos.

appendix_digests.title: A Dozen Grammatical Rules You Absolutely Need to Know

rules.claim: And or but may begin a sentence and can provide concise continuity.
A sentence may end with a preposition when that phrasing is natural, though sentence endings deserve emphasis.
Use well, rather than good, as the ordinary adverb describing performance or manner.
The true grammatical subject controls verb number, including in inverted and interrupted constructions.
Either and neither take singular verbs when each is the subject.
With either-or and neither-nor subjects of mixed number, match the verb to the nearer alternative.
Do not add an unnecessary -ly ending to established flat adverbs.
Conjunctive adverbs such as however do not join independent clauses with a comma alone.
An adverb in a verb phrase usually reads naturally after the first auxiliary.
Keep a relative pronoun close to its antecedent to prevent ambiguous reference.
Paired correlative conjunctions require parallel grammatical structures.
Set off a nonessential appositive, but do not separate an appositive necessary to identify its referent.

appendix_digests.title: A Dozen Punctuation Rules You Absolutely Need to Know

rules.claim: Hyphenate multiword modifiers before nouns when needed to show they function as one adjective, subject to stated exceptions.
Use a serial comma consistently to reduce ambiguity in lists.
Do not insert a comma between two predicates sharing one subject; punctuate longer or internally complex series for clarity.
Do not normally use apostrophes to form plurals.

rules.locator: Appendix C > subject and verb proximity
rules.claim: Keep the grammatical subject and verb reasonably close unless an intentionally set-off modifier intervenes.
Use bullets for scannable parallel lists, with a clear setup and restrained visual treatment; overuse weakens emphasis.
Do not use quotation marks merely for emphasis because they can imply quotation, irony, or doubt.
Most prefixed American English terms are closed, with hyphens reserved for ambiguity, proper nouns, or conventional prefixes.
Use a colon or comma after a salutation according to context, not a semicolon.
Em-dashes can frame or emphasize interruptive matter but lose force when overused.
Punctuate month-year and full-date constructions according to their components rather than inserting a comma automatically.
Form singular possessives with apostrophe-s in the source's stated style, including most singular words ending in s sounds.

appendix_digests.title: Common Usage Gaffes
high_value_rules: Use adverbs and adjectives according to function, including do well and feel bad.
Use objective pronoun forms after prepositions and as verb objects.
Use couldn't care less for complete indifference.
Distinguish lie from lay and their inflected forms.
Avoid redundant terminal prepositions in constructions such as asking where something is.
Use the past perfect in counterfactual conditions about an earlier event.
Use as such only when it refers to a previously stated status.
Prefer by accident, could have, in regard to or regarding, fewer for countable items, preventive, regardless, and standard subject-verb agreement.
appendix_digests.constraint: These are usage checkpoints, not substitutes for evaluating clarity, accuracy, or audience fit.

appendix_digests.title: Some Dos and Don'ts of Business-Writing Etiquette
dos: Verify names, honorifics, addresses, recipients, and referenced attachments.
Use white space, margins, paragraphs, and subheads to reduce visual strain.
Date non-email correspondence for later reference.
Personalize multiple thank-you notes sent within the same group.
donts: Do not use all caps as extended emphasis.
Do not thank someone in advance as a substitute for thanking them after completion.
Do not use BCC casually when it could appear indiscreet.
Do not use tiny, unusual fonts or overlong email subjects.
Do not let delay prevent a sincere note of thanks, congratulations, or condolence.
Do not write while angry; regain enough distance to communicate calmly.
Do not put in writing material you could not responsibly defend if made public.
appendix_digests.constraint: Some medium-specific etiquette reflects the book's 2012 context and should be adapted to current channels without losing its underlying care, privacy, and readability principles.

operationally_relevant_distinctions.claim: Distinguish taking something up from modifying it.
Distinguish unfavorable conditions from reluctance or opposition.
Usually use affect as the influence verb and effect as the result noun, while recognizing effect as a bring-about verb.
Distinguish multiple possible meanings from mixed feelings.
Distinguish valuation from keeping someone informed.
Distinguish reassuring a person, making an outcome certain, and indemnifying against loss.
Use between for one-to-one relationships and among for a looser group relationship.
Distinguish working together from confirming evidence.
Use comprise for including parts and composed of for being made from parts; avoid is comprised of under the source's guidance.
Distinguish recurring events from uninterrupted duration.
The source distinguishes convincing someone of a proposition from persuading someone to act.
Distinguish believable, gullible, unbelieving, and respectable.
Distinguish literal designation from associated implication.
Distinguish impartiality from lack of interest.
Distinguish what is stated unambiguously from what is implied or assumed.
A communicator implies; a recipient infers.
Use less for amounts and fewer for countable units.
Distinguish reciprocal relationships from shared characteristics or interests.
Distinguish usefulness in practice from basic feasibility.
Distinguish directing a course from forbidding one.
Distinguish main person or amount from a rule or belief.
Distinguish answering a claim from disproving it.
Distinguish big-picture planning from actions that support the plan.
The source prefers that for restrictive clauses and which with commas for nonrestrictive clauses.
Prefer the shorter ordinary verb use when it conveys the intended meaning.
Omit or not when it adds nothing; retain it when the sense is regardless of the alternative.
